title: Brennan's
intro: The house on Royal Street, its breakfast, its sauces and the dishes it made famous. Every entry ties a classical idea to a plate you will carry to the table.

entries.title: The Brennan's sauce family
entries.say: As it reads: the Brennan's sauce family.
entries.summary: Every sauce on the Brennan's menus placed in the family it comes from: the warm egg emulsions, the brown sauces, the butter sauces, the Creole sauces, the bistro and raw bar sauces, and the sweet sauces of dessert.
entries.guest: Most of our plates are built around a classic sauce: the egg dishes carry hollandaise and its cousins, the breakfast steak béarnaise, and the Creole plates a peppery butter or tomato sauce.

paras: Almost every plate at Brennan's is built around a sauce, and almost every sauce belongs to a family: a small group of sauces made the same way from the same base. Learn the family and you know how a sauce is made, tastes and fails before you learn a recipe. Each sauce has its own entry.

The house guide says the sauce usually matters more than the protein. For the guest, a mild fish or lean tenderloin tastes mostly of its sauce; for the wine, the sauce sets the match: hollandaise wants acid and bubbles, a red wine sauce welcomes a red.

Kitchens teach five mother sauces: espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate and hollandaise. Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903) named four grandes sauces de base, the first four, and set hollandaise among the warm emulsified sauces, fat and liquid held as one smooth sauce. Carême, earlier, counted espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel.

The French classics. Hollandaise is egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon or a vinegar reduction. Built on a vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction it becomes béarnaise; with tomato paste folded in, béarnaise becomes Choron; with glace de viande, a syrupy meat glaze, it becomes Foyot. The brown family gives marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce: red wine and brown stock, in New Orleans often bound with a roux, flour cooked in fat. The butter sauces give beurre blanc, cold butter whisked into a sharp wine and shallot reduction, with no yolk.

The Creole side. Creole sauce is the city's tomato sauce on the holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, carrying tasso on the shrimp and grits. New Orleans barbecue sauce is a buttery, peppery pan sauce in the barbecue shrimp style, not smoky and not tomato, on the Louisiana Oysters; the BBQ Lobster carries one in the same style, confirmed at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service. A chive rémoulade, a cold spiced sauce, comes with the Crawfish Meat Pies.

The bistro and the bar. A mustard cream sauce, shallot, wine and cream with mustard stirred in off the heat, on the Poussin; mignonette, shallot in vinegar with cracked pepper, on the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters; brown butter, cooked until its milk solids toast nutty, as a warm vinaigrette on the Crab Claws; a gastrique, caramel loosened with vinegar, made with Crystal hot sauce for the Popcorn Shrimp; and the Creole Caesar's dressing, an emulsion in the Caesar way with smoked oysters taking anchovy's usual briny role.

The sweet sauces. A crème anglaise, the stirred pouring custard, made with sweetened condensed milk for the Pineapple Tarte Tatin; a whiskey caramel on the bread pudding; and the Foster's blond caramel of butter and brown sugar, lit with rum at the table.

What binds a sauce decides how it is held. Egg yolk binds the warm emulsions, made in small batches and held warm, around 60°C (140°F), and cold ones too, such as the Caesar dressing and a mayonnaise rémoulade. Butter alone binds beurre blanc and the barbecue sauce, which break if they boil or sit. Roux and reduction give body to the brown and tomato sauces, which can simmer and hold. Acid alone carries the mignonette, yolk heated to about 82°C (180°F) sets the anglaise, and sugar cooked to caramel carries the caramels.

The pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish needs a question first, because bordelaise names two sauces: in the French kitchen a red wine sauce with shallot, demi-glace, a glossy reduced brown sauce, and bone marrow; in New Orleans usually a garlic butter with parsley. Confirm which with the kitchen before you pair a wine: a red wine sauce changes the bottle.

The Brennan's sauces folio sets six of the menu's sauces side by side, classic studies, not photographs of our plates: hollandaise pale yellow; béarnaise flecked with tarragon; Choron soft coral; Foyot tan from its glaze; marchand de vin glossy red-brown; beurre blanc ivory. Learn them by colour.
Each family fails its own way: a warm emulsion scrambles when too hot and splits when too cool, a butter sauce breaks when it boils, a roux scorches bitter, and caramel burns in seconds.

Name the sauce in plain words first and the French second: a buttery, lemony egg-yolk sauce, hollandaise. House recipes are not printed, so recipe questions go to the kitchen. Mention the alcohol in the whiskey caramel and the Foster to a guest who avoids it: flaming burns the vapour, not all the rum.

brennans.how: The Eggs Hussarde carries two families on one plate: marchand de vin, the dark, winey brown sauce, beneath the egg, and hollandaise, the bright warm emulsion, on top.
On the Eggs Sardou, Choron, béarnaise finished with tomato, takes the place of the usual hollandaise: coral, tangy and herbal, brighter than hollandaise.
Foyot, béarnaise with glace de viande whisked in, brings tawny, savoury depth to the Roasted Chateaubriand, a lean, mild cut that needs a rich sauce.
The breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak carries French béarnaise, hollandaise built on a vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction: the classic sharp, herbal sauce for beef.
The Redfish Véronique carries a preserved lemon beurre blanc: cold butter whisked into a sharp reduction with no yolk, salty and perfumed over a firm, mild fish.
The pecan bordelaise is most likely the New Orleans garlic butter with toasted pecans rather than the French red wine sauce; confirm with the kitchen before pairing a wine.
Creole sauce, the city's tomato sauce on the holy trinity, carries tasso on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, so it is smoky as well as tangy.
The Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch come in New Orleans barbecue sauce: a buttery, peppery pan sauce in the barbecue shrimp style, neither smoky nor tomato.
The Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the dinner tasting carries a New Orleans barbecue sauce in the same buttery, peppery style; the recipe is not published, so confirm the kitchen's version at lineup.
The Grand Isle Jewel Oysters come with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette with parsley: shallot, vinegar and cracked pepper, spooned on by the guest at the table.
On the Louisiana Crab Claws, brown butter becomes a warm vinaigrette: butter cooked until its milk solids toast nutty, then sharpened with acid.
The Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost come with a chive rémoulade, cool, tangy and herby against hot pastry; which rémoulade style it follows, the kitchen can say.
The Popcorn Shrimp at the Roost come with a Crystal gastrique, a sweet and sour reduction made with the New Orleans hot sauce: sweet, tangy and gently spicy for dipping.
The Poussin à la Moutarde puts a Burgundian bistro mustard cream sauce over a sweet tea-brined, fried Cornish hen: a French sauce on a Southern bird.
Beside the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, a crème anglaise made with sweetened condensed milk brings a caramel note, cool and silky against hot caramel and pastry.

The Creole Caesar's dressing is a Caesar emulsion with smoked oysters blended in, taking the briny role anchovy usually plays; whether it also carries anchovy is for the chef. Treat it as a shellfish dish, flag it on the ticket and check with the kitchen.
The New Orleans Bread Pudding carries a whiskey caramel, amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, with whiskey for warmth; mention the alcohol to a guest who avoids it.

cards.front: Name the six families of the Brennan's sauces, with a sauce from each.
cards.back: Warm egg emulsions (hollandaise and its cousins), brown (marchand de vin), butter (beurre blanc), Creole (Creole sauce, barbecue sauce, rémoulade), bistro and bar (mustard cream, mignonette, a Crystal gastrique of caramel, vinegar and hot sauce) and sweet (anglaise, caramels).

cards.front: Which four menu sauces belong to the hollandaise family?
cards.back: Hollandaise on the Hussarde and the Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, Choron on the Sardou and Foyot on the Chateaubriand. Escoffier's 1903 Guide named four base sauces and set hollandaise among the warm emulsions; later teaching made it the fifth mother sauce.

cards.front: How do Choron and Foyot each change béarnaise?
cards.back: Choron folds in tomato cooked to a paste, turning it coral and tangy; Foyot whisks in glace de viande, a meat glaze, turning it tan and savoury.

cards.front: Which family does marchand de vin come from?
cards.back: The brown family: red wine reduced with brown stock, in New Orleans with onion, garlic and often mushroom, and often bound with a roux.

cards.front: What holds a beurre blanc together when it has no egg yolk?
cards.back: Cold butter whisked piece by piece into a sharp wine, vinegar and shallot reduction over low heat. Ours is preserved lemon, on the Redfish Véronique.

cards.front: Is New Orleans barbecue sauce smoky or tomato-based?
cards.back: Neither: it is a buttery, peppery pan sauce in the barbecue shrimp style, on the Louisiana Oysters and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster.

cards.front: Why is the pecan bordelaise the sauce to confirm?
cards.back: Bordelaise names two sauces, the French red wine sauce and the New Orleans garlic butter. Ask the kitchen which it is before pairing a wine.

cards.front: Why learn the sauce on a plate before the protein?
cards.back: The sauce usually decides how a dish tastes and what wine it wants: hollandaise wants acid and bubbles, a red wine sauce welcomes a red.

cards.front: What is a mignonette, and which oysters carry ours?
cards.back: Shallot in vinegar with cracked pepper, spooned on raw oysters. Ours adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley, on the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, which are served raw: give the consumer advisory the service note carries.

cards.front: Name three sweet sauces and the desserts they go with.
cards.back: The sweetened condensed anglaise with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, the whiskey caramel on the bread pudding, and the rum-lit caramel of the Bananas Foster.

cards.front: How does each family's binding change the way the kitchen holds it?
cards.back: Warm emulsions are made in small batches and held warm, about 60°C (140°F); butter sauces break if they boil; roux and tomato sauces can simmer and hold.

cards.front: What makes the Creole Caesar dressing different?
cards.back: Smoked oysters are blended into the Caesar emulsion, taking anchovy's usual briny role; whether it also carries anchovy is for the chef. Flag it as a shellfish dish on the ticket and check with the kitchen.

questions.q: Which of these sauces is not a member of the hollandaise family?
questions.answer: Marchand de vin
questions.why: Béarnaise, Choron and Foyot are all built on the warm yolk and butter emulsion; marchand de vin is a red wine brown sauce.

questions.q: Which sauce is béarnaise finished with tomato?
questions.answer: Choron
questions.why: Choron folds tomato paste into béarnaise; Foyot adds meat glaze, Paloise swaps the tarragon for mint, and Maltaise is hollandaise with blood orange.

questions.q: Which family does the marchand de vin on the egg dishes come from?
questions.answer: The brown sauces
questions.why: Marchand de vin is red wine reduced with brown stock, in New Orleans often bound with a roux, so it sits in the brown family.

questions.q: How would you describe the New Orleans barbecue sauce on the Louisiana Oysters?
questions.answer: Buttery and peppery
questions.why: New Orleans barbecue sauce is a pan sauce of butter and black pepper in the barbecue shrimp style, never smoky and never tomato-based.

questions.answer: Which bordelaise it carries

questions.answer: The anchovy's briny role

questions.answer: Among the warm emulsified sauces

Among the cold sauces of the larder

entries.title: Eggs Hussarde
entries.summary: The Brennan's signature egg dish: poached eggs on coffee-cured Canadian bacon and housemade English muffins, with marchand de vin, a red wine sauce, beneath and hollandaise on top. New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict, under a name older than the restaurant.
entries.guest: Eggs Hussarde is our signature egg dish: our own English muffins, coffee-cured Canadian bacon and poached eggs, with two sauces, buttery hollandaise and a savoury red wine sauce.

paras: Eggs Hussarde is poached eggs on Canadian bacon over a toasted bread base, with two sauces: marchand de vin, a dark red wine sauce, beneath the egg, and hollandaise, the warm butter and egg-yolk sauce, on top. At Brennan's it is the signature egg dish and the egg course of the Traditional Breakfast, built on housemade English muffins and coffee-cured Canadian bacon.

Think of it as New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict. The Benedict has one sauce; the Hussarde adds a second, deep and winey, so every forkful carries something bright and something rich. For a new cook it is three classical foundations on one plate.

Hussarde is French for hussar style. The hussars were light cavalry, first raised in Hungary, and why the dish took their name is not known. The name is older than the restaurant: a recipe for poached eggs à la Hussarde was printed in 1895, credited to the chef Adolphe Gallier of the Hotel Brunswick in New York, and Escoffier gave a version in Le Guide Culinaire in 1903. The two-sauce plate is the New Orleans form, which Brennan's made famous from about 1950. So call it our signature, and never say it was invented here.
The house guide credits Paul Blangé, the first chef, with the Brennan's Hussarde; confirm that wording with a manager at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service, before you tell it.

A kitchen builds it in parts that meet at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen. The eggs are poached in water held just below a simmer, about 85°C (185°F), often with a splash of vinegar, for about three minutes, until the white is set and the yolk still runs. Many kitchens poach ahead, hold the eggs in iced water and rewarm them to order for 30 seconds to a minute in hot water, well below a simmer. The bacon is warmed, the muffin split and toasted, and both sauces wait at the station: the marchand de vin hot, the hollandaise warm, around 60°C (140°F), never hot.

The house guide gives the stack from the bottom: English muffin, coffee-cured Canadian bacon, marchand de vin, poached egg, hollandaise. The guide also speaks of the sauces side by side, so confirm tonight's plating at the pass. In the classic build the two sauces stay distinct: the brown sauce goes on first, under the egg, and the hollandaise last, over it, so the pale sauce rests on the egg instead of sinking into the dark one.

Each part rests on a foundation taught in its own entry. The egg is poaching. The marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce, comes from the brown family: in the New Orleans way, onion and plenty of garlic in place of the shallot, often ham and mushroom, beef stock and red wine, frequently bound with a roux, flour cooked in fat. The hollandaise is the warm emulsion, egg yolk holding butter in a smooth, lemony sauce.

What goes wrong at the pass: a hard yolk, from an egg poached too long or warmed too hot; a ragged white, from water at a rolling boil or a tired egg; a hollandaise that is greasy or grainy, from a sauce held too hot or too cool; sauces that run together, from too much of either. Each is a reason to cook the plate again, a refire, never to send it.

At Brennan's the base is housemade English muffins, split so their craggy holes catch both sauces. The classic Brennan's Hussarde was built on Holland rusks, dry, crisp toasts; a returning guest may notice the change. Canadian bacon is cured, lightly smoked pork loin; a coffee cure rubs it with salt, sugar and ground coffee, which gives the lean meat a roasty, slightly bitter depth. How long it cures, whether it is made in house, and whether tonight's marchand de vin carries ham or mushroom are questions for the chef.

Say it hoo-SARD, and the red wine sauce marchand de vin, mar-SHAHN duh VAN. Lead a guest's first breakfast with it, and offer it to anyone who loves Eggs Benedict. Describe it as rich, buttery and savoury, with a deep, winey note and a bright, lemony edge. The yolks come soft: check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs, and send every allergen question to the kitchen and the service note. Do not confuse it with Eggs Owen, which shares the two sauces over short rib débris.

brennans.how: Soft poached eggs sit on coffee-cured Canadian bacon over a split housemade English muffin; the classic house build used Holland rusks, and the stacking is confirmed at the pass.
Marchand de vin, the dark, winey brown sauce, goes beneath the egg and hollandaise, the bright warm emulsion, over it, so each forkful carries one deep sauce and one bright one.

Hussarde is hussar style, after the light cavalry. A recipe under the name was printed in 1895 and Escoffier gave one in 1903; Brennan's made the two-sauce plate famous from about 1950, so it is our signature, never our invention.

entries.title: Eggs Sardou
entries.summary: Poached eggs on artichokes with creamed spinach, a New Orleans classic born at Antoine's and named for the playwright Victorien Sardou. Brennan's sets the eggs on crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach under Choron, a béarnaise with tomato.
entries.guest: Eggs Sardou is a New Orleans classic: poached eggs with crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach, finished with Choron, a tangy béarnaise brightened with tomato.

paras: Eggs Sardou is poached eggs set on artichokes, usually with creamed spinach, under a warm butter sauce. It is one of the classic New Orleans egg dishes, and Brennan's serves it at breakfast and lunch as a signature. It is not a Brennan's invention: it was born at Antoine's, the French Quarter restaurant opened in 1840, and Brennan's serves it in its own style.

For a new cook the plate is a lesson in contrast: soft egg against crisp artichoke, rich spinach against a tangy sauce. For a server it is the only one of the three house egg dishes, with the Hussarde and the Owen, that has no meat printed on its menu line, a natural partner to a Hussarde across the table; a guest who asks whether it suits a particular diet goes to the kitchen.

Antoine's created the dish and named it in honour of Victorien Sardou, the French playwright, and the story ties it to a visit to New Orleans. Sources disagree on the year, and whether he ever ate it there belongs to the legend: say named for him, not created for him. Antoine's original set poached eggs on artichoke bottoms, the cup-shaped base of the heart, with hollandaise, ham, anchovy and truffle, and no spinach at all. Most later versions dropped the ham, anchovy and truffle for creamed spinach, and that is the version Brennan's made its own.

In the Brennan's style the plate is four preparations brought together at the pass, the counter where the kitchen finishes plates and hands them to the servers. The artichoke hearts are trimmed, cooked until tender, then coated and fried crisp in oil at about 175 to 190°C (347 to 374°F), drained on a rack and kept hot; the classic Sardou used cooked artichoke bottoms, and the crisp coating is the house's change. The spinach is blanched, plunged into iced water, squeezed hard, chopped and bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel, then finished with Parmesan and often a little nutmeg.

The eggs are poached for about three minutes in water just below a simmer, until the white sets and the yolk runs. The Choron is made in small batches and held warm, around 60°C (140°F), never hot. In the classic build the spinach goes down first, the artichoke sits on it, the egg sits in or on the artichoke, and the sauce goes over the egg. The house's own plating is confirmed at the pass.

Each part rests on a foundation. The eggs are poaching. The artichokes are frying: a coating dries and browns into a crust while the inside steams. The creamed spinach is bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel, the white sauce of milk thickened with a roux; squeezing out the water is the step that keeps it rich, not watery. The sauce is the béarnaise family. Béarnaise is hollandaise built on a vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction; Choron is béarnaise finished with tomato cooked down to a thick paste, so it turns a soft coral and tastes tangy and herbal, brighter than hollandaise.

The faults to catch at the pass are soggy artichokes, from oil too cool or from sitting under sauce too long; watery spinach, not squeezed dry, which bleeds green water across the plate; a hard yolk; and a split or thin Choron. Each means cooking the plate again, a refire, never sending it.

The Brennan's Sardou sets poached eggs over crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach, with Choron in place of hollandaise. On an American menu Parmesan is a generic name for a hard grating cheese, so until the chef says which cheese goes in, call it Parmesan and nothing grander. The crispy artichokes are likely breaded or floured before frying, and any question about the coating goes to the kitchen. Whether the Sardou's spinach is the same preparation as the creamed spinach side is worth confirming before you say so.

Say it sar-DOO, and Choron sho-ROHN. Describe Choron as a béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, brightened with tomato: tangy and herbal. Offer the Sardou to a guest who loves artichokes or creamed spinach, or who wants an egg dish without the Canadian bacon. Never present it as a Brennan's invention: it is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style. Questions about allergens, the coating or a diet go to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: Eggs Owen
entries.summary: Short rib débris braised in red wine and pulled, with a Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg, under the Hussarde's two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin. The hearty plate of the Brennan's breakfast and lunch menu: steak and eggs, New Orleans style.
entries.guest: Eggs Owen is short rib braised in red wine until it falls apart, with a Creole-spiced potato, a soft-boiled egg and our two sauces: steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

paras: Eggs Owen is short rib débris, beef braised slowly in red wine and pulled into its own gravy, with a Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg, finished with the same two sauces as the Eggs Hussarde: hollandaise and marchand de vin. On the breakfast and lunch menu it is the heartier plate, steak and eggs in the New Orleans way, for the hungry guest or the table that wants red wine at breakfast.

Guests often guess the name honours Owen Brennan, who founded the restaurant in 1946. The menu does not say so and the house has not published that story, so it is confirmed at lineup before it is told. Until then, describe the plate and let the name wait.

Débris, said DAY-bree, is Louisiana French for scraps. In New Orleans it means the shreds of meat that fall into the gravy as a roast cooks and is carved, and it is best known on the roast beef po-boy: Mother's Restaurant on Poydras Street, open since 1938, made the word famous. The Brennan's débris takes the same idea and makes it richer, with short rib in place of the roast.

The following red wine braise is a general teaching model, not a confirmed Brennan's production recipe. Short rib has connective tissue that softens during slow, moist cooking. In a browned braise, the ribs are seasoned and seared, aromatics cooked, and the pan deglazed with wine before cooking liquid is added. The covered pot cooks gently until the intended tenderness is reached. Cut size, equipment and recipe determine time and liquid level; the house method is confirmed at the pass.

For pulled débris, the cooked meat is separated from bone, gristle and excess fat, then pulled. The cooking liquid can be strained, skimmed and reduced before the meat is returned. Pulling is the intended texture here, although another braised dish may need pieces that lift out whole. Finish and holding follow the actual kitchen recipe.

The menu specifies a soft-boiled egg. A runny centre depends on egg size, starting temperature and cooking method, so six minutes is not a universal house standard. The kitchen confirms its timing, cooling, reheating and service process. The Creole-spiced potato's cut and cooking method also need confirmation at the pass.

Its foundations are three: the red wine braise, the warm emulsion of hollandaise, and the brown family's marchand de vin, often bound with a roux. Set it beside the Hussarde and the differences are the lesson: braised beef for the Canadian bacon, a potato for the English muffin, and a soft-boiled egg for a poached one. The sauces are the same, so the two plates taste of one kitchen, but the Owen is deeper and meatier.
The Hussarde illustration linked below is a comparison of components, not a picture of Eggs Owen. It shows the muffin, bacon and poached-egg arrangement that this dish replaces.

Tough or dry débris needs a check of the cut, heat, cooking time and holding conditions. A greasy gravy may need skimming, while sauce body depends on the intended recipe. A firm yolk does not match the requested soft centre; assess the egg and the actual cooking process rather than diagnosing it from a universal six-minute rule.

The Brennan's Eggs Owen takes the Hussarde's two sauces, hollandaise for butter and lemon and marchand de vin for depth, over red wine-braised short rib débris and a Creole-spiced potato, topped with a soft-boiled egg. Older write-ups describe a poached egg and hash version that is gone, so use the current menu wording only. The house blend of Creole spice is not printed: describe it as warm and savoury rather than fiery, and send any question about a particular spice, or the heat, to the kitchen.

Say débris DAY-bree, and describe it as slow-cooked beef that falls apart into its own gravy. Offer the Owen to a guest who wants steak and eggs, or who finds the Hussarde too delicate. The braise and the marchand de vin both carry red wine, so a soft red makes sense here even at breakfast. Never tell the Owen Brennan story unless lineup has confirmed it, and send allergen questions to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: The Brennan's Turtle Soup
entries.summary: Brennan's signature soup at breakfast, lunch and dinner: a dark, roux-thickened Creole soup of 100 per cent turtle meat, built on the trinity and a rich stock, finished with aged sherry, brown butter spinach and grated egg.
entries.guest: Our Turtle Soup is a Brennan's classic: 100 per cent turtle meat in a rich, dark Creole soup, with brown butter spinach, grated egg and a splash of aged sherry.

paras: Turtle soup is the bowl that tells a guest what Brennan's is about: a dark, thick Creole soup, long cooked, served at breakfast, lunch and dinner and as the second course of the Traditional Breakfast. For many guests it is the first turtle they have eaten, so say the word plainly and describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep, finely chopped stew.

The menu prints 100 per cent turtle meat, and the words matter. Many turtle soups, in restaurants and in cans, are stretched with veal or beef, and mock turtle has no turtle at all. Ours is all turtle: dark, firm meat full of gelatine, somewhere between veal and dark chicken, and that gelatine, with the roux, gives the soup its body.

This is the Creole build, taught step by step in Creole turtle soup; how our kitchen does each step, and how dark it takes the roux, is a chef question. A brown roux, flour cooked in fat to the colour of milk chocolate until it smells of toasted nuts, meets the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper; tomato, a rich brown stock and finely chopped turtle follow, the stock a ladle at a time, and the soup simmers gently, skimmed, until it coats a spoon.

Roux and stock meet at different temperatures, never both hot, so the flour disperses before it swells. The classic proportion is about 115 g (4 oz) each of fat and flour to 2 litres (about 2 quarts) of stock, more than a pale sauce would need, since a brown roux thickens less. The turtle needs a long, gentle simmer, often well over an hour, until it is tender; the soup then takes a further 45 minutes to an hour at a lazy bubble, about 90°C (194°F), to cook out the flour and bring the flavours together. How our kitchen times it is a chef question.

The finish comes last. Lemon juice brightens it, hard-boiled egg enriches it, spinach brings colour and an earthy note, and dry, aged sherry cuts the richness the way lemon lifts fish. Hold the finished soup at 57°C (135°F) or above, the FDA Food Code figure for hot holding.

A turtle soup fails in the roux and in the simmer. A roux with black flecks or an acrid smell makes the whole pot bitter, and no seasoning hides it: start again. Hot stock poured all at once into a hot roux turns lumpy. A hard boil makes the soup greasy and the meat stringy. A dark soup that stays thin needs more roux, and a flat one wants salt, lemon or the sherry.

At Brennan's the soup is made with snapping turtle, a freshwater turtle, by the house guide's account, chopped finely and simmered long so it spreads through the soup. Louisiana closed the wild alligator snapper to commercial trappers, so restaurants buy from licensed farms or collectors; whether ours is farm-raised, and from whom, is a question for the chef, confirmed at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service, before you name anyone.

Spinach wilted in brown butter, nutty and soft, is folded through, and hard-boiled egg is grated over the top; the body comes from the roux and the gelatine, not the egg. Aged sherry finishes it, and whether it goes in at the stove, at the pass (the counter where plates leave the kitchen) or at the table is a lineup question.

Builders found turtles in the courtyard during the 2014 restoration, and the house adopted them. Ten live there now, named for sauces: five for the French mother sauces as kitchens teach them, from béchamel to hollandaise, and five for New Orleans sauces. Say it before a guest asks, with a smile: the soup is not the turtles.

Offer the soup to every first visit and to anyone who asks what New Orleans tastes like. Sherry is in the bowl, so tell a guest avoiding alcohol before they order, and never promise that it cooks off. The soup carries egg, butter in the spinach and, in the Creole tradition, a wheat flour roux, so every allergen question goes to the service note and the kitchen. On the Traditional Breakfast the guest chooses this or the Seafood Gumbo, and either comes with a Bloody Bull, a Bloody Mary made with beef bouillon: both are soups, so read the ticket twice.

entries.title: The Brennan's Seafood Gumbo
entries.summary: Brennan's signature gumbo: shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, simmered into a dark-roux Creole seafood gumbo over Louisiana popcorn rice, served at breakfast, lunch and dinner and as a soup choice on the Traditional Breakfast.
entries.guest: Our Seafood Gumbo is shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille sausage, over Louisiana popcorn rice: savoury, briny and smoky, with gentle spice.

paras: Gumbo, GUM-boh, is the dish that says Louisiana: a dark stew usually built on a roux and served with rice. Its name most likely comes from a West African word for okra, its roux from French cooking taken darker in Louisiana, and its filé, ground sassafras leaves, from the Choctaw. Roux is one of three thickeners: okra, simmered, gives a silky body, and filé is stirred in off the heat or at the table, because boiling turns it stringy. Many gumbos use a roux with one of the others, and some use okra or filé alone. A seafood gumbo stands on a stock made from the shells, and the seafood goes in at the very end.

Ours is a Brennan's signature at breakfast, lunch and dinner: shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, over Louisiana popcorn rice, and the alternative to the turtle soup on the Traditional Breakfast. It tastes savoury, briny and smoky, with gentle spice: sweetness from the seafood, smoke and warmth from the sausage.

The full technique belongs to Seafood gumbo; here is the order of the build. First a stock from the shrimp shells and crab bodies, kept short so it never turns bitter; then a dark roux of flour and oil, stirred to the colour of dark chocolate; then the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, which stops the roux browning, with garlic, the browned andouille and the stock, a ladle at a time; then a gentle simmer, skimmed. The seafood goes in last, by the time each needs: FDA guidance cooks seafood to 63°C (145°F), when shrimp turn pearly and opaque and oysters plump, while the picked crab, already cooked, is only heated through.

Most gumbo faults start in the roux. Black flecks or an acrid smell mean it burnt, and the gumbo will taste bitter: start again. A dark gumbo that stays thin needs more roux, because a dark roux thickens less; a pasty, muddy one had too much, or too short a simmer to cook out the flour. A greasy surface was never skimmed. Rubbery shrimp and shrunken oysters were cooked too long or held in the pot, and a harsh stock sat too long on its shells.

The menu prints shrimp, crab, oysters, andouille and popcorn rice, and names no source for the seafood, so where today's comes from is a kitchen question. Gulf shrimp, brown or white by season, want only a couple of minutes. Picked lump crab is sweet and already cooked, so it is only warmed. Gulf oysters are large and mild from brackish water. Andouille is a coarse, heavily smoked pork sausage, made to season a pot rather than to eat alone. Popcorn rice is a Louisiana aromatic long grain that smells of popcorn as it cooks and keeps its grains firm and separate in the broth.

Brennan's published gumbo recipe starts from a dark mahogany roux with andouille and okra in crab stock, and carries tomato and filé, but the menu prints none of those, so never promise them: say published recipe, never menu, and only once the chef confirms at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service, that the dining room gumbo follows it.

Suggest the gumbo to seafood lovers, to a guest who wants something hearty before an egg dish, and to anyone choosing a soup on the Traditional Breakfast, where either soup comes with a Bloody Bull, a Bloody Mary made with beef bouillon. The spice is mild to moderate. Every spoonful carries shrimp, crab and oysters, the andouille is pork and gumbo is usually built on a wheat flour roux, so every allergen or diet question goes to the service note and the kitchen before the guest orders. A toasty smell as the bowl lands is the rice.

entries.title: Redfish Véronique
entries.summary: The dinner menu's French classic with a Gulf fish: redfish with hibiscus-pickled grapes, braised leeks, fingerling potatoes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc. It is Brennan's take on Sole Véronique and the third course of the dinner tasting.
entries.guest: Our Redfish Véronique is the French classic of fish with grapes: redfish with hibiscus-pickled grapes, braised leeks, fingerling potatoes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc.

paras: À la Véronique, vay-ro-NEEK, means served with grapes. The classic is Sole Véronique: poached sole in a creamy white wine sauce with peeled green muscat grapes, glazed under the grill. Tradition credits it to Escoffier and names it for André Messager's operetta Véronique, first staged in Paris in 1898, but the chef and the date vary between tellings, so tell it as a story rather than a fact.

Brennan's keeps the idea and makes three changes: redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and grapes pickled with hibiscus for fresh ones, over braised leeks and fingerling potatoes. It is a dinner main course and the third course of the dinner tasting, and it teaches three foundations at once: cooking a fillet, mounting a butter sauce and balancing acid.

Redfish, the red drum, has firm, mild, slightly sweet white flesh that holds together in a hot pan. A firm fillet like this is usually sautéed or pan-roasted: the pan and a little fat hot, the presentation side down first and left alone to colour, turned once and finished gently, in the oven if thick. FDA guidance cooks fish to 63°C (145°F), when the flesh turns opaque and flakes at a touch. How our kitchen cooks it is learned at lineup, the short staff meeting before each service.

A beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, starts as a reduction: about 100 ml (about 7 tbsp) of white wine and 50 ml (about 3 tbsp) of white wine vinegar with a finely chopped shallot, reduced to roughly 30 ml (2 tbsp). Over low heat, about 225 g (8 oz) of cold, diced butter is whisked in a few pieces at a time, so it softens into a creamy emulsion rather than melting into oil. Finely chopped preserved lemon rind, salty and perfumed, goes in at the end.

The sauce is held warm, about 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F), off direct heat: much hotter and the butter oils out, much cooler and it sets. The low end sits below 57°C (135°F), the FDA Food Code line for hot holding, so the kitchen makes it in small batches and replaces it on a schedule the chef sets rather than holding it all service.

Pickled grapes are steeped in a sweet and sour brine; a common kitchen method pours hot vinegar, water and sugar over halved grapes, and dried hibiscus in the brine turns them ruby and adds a tart, cranberry-like note. The balance is the lesson: butter and leek bring richness and sweetness, preserved lemon brings salt and perfume, the grapes bring sharpness and fruit. Taste the sauce and a grape together before the plate goes.

A beurre blanc fails by heat. Too hot, and the butter oils out into a greasy, separated sauce; too cool, and it sets thick and waxy. A sauce that is only starting to split can often be brought back off the heat by whisking it, a little at a time, into a spoonful of fresh reduction or cold cream in a clean pan. The fish fails by time: well past 63°C (145°F), redfish dries and tightens. The plate fails by balance: season the sauce after the preserved lemon goes in, never before, or it ends up salty.

On our plate: redfish, a firm, mild fish that lets the grapes and sauce speak; hibiscus-pickled grapes, sweet, tart and floral, in place of fresh muscat; braised leeks, soft and gently sweet, and fingerling potatoes, small and waxy, as the quiet base; and a preserved lemon beurre blanc. Where our redfish comes from is a question for the chef. Louisiana has barred the commercial catch of wild redfish since the late 1980s, after the blackened redfish craze, so restaurant redfish is farmed or comes from other sources.

Offer it to a guest who wants fish at dinner, something elegant and light, or a French classic with a local fish. If a guest is wary of fruit with fish, describe the grapes as a sharp relish rather than a sweet garnish. The plate is fish in a butter sauce, so every allergen question goes to the service note and the kitchen. On the dinner tasting the course is paired with a light red Burgundy, the printed Beaune Premier Cru; confirm the open bottle at lineup, and be ready to say why a light, low-tannin red suits the hibiscus grapes.

entries.title: Pecan Gulf Fish
entries.summary: A breakfast and lunch main course: the Gulf fish of the day topped with Louisiana lump crab, with a pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens. Today's fish, which bordelaise, and every nut or shellfish question are settled with the kitchen.
entries.guest: Our Pecan Gulf Fish is today's local catch, topped with Louisiana lump crab, with a nutty pecan bordelaise, a silky cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens.

paras: The Pecan Gulf Fish is the Gulf fish plate of the breakfast and lunch menu: the day's catch topped with Louisiana lump crab, sauced with a pecan bordelaise and set over a cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens. It eats lighter than the egg dishes but still satisfies: nutty, buttery and sweet from the crab, with earthy greens.

Two things make it a Chef de Partie dish. The fish changes with what the boats bring, so it is learned at lineup, never guessed. And bordelaise means two different sauces: in a French kitchen a red wine sauce, in a New Orleans dining room usually a garlic butter. Which one the kitchen means changes the wine you pour.

Gulf fish means the day's catch, drum, sheepshead, snapper, grouper, triggerfish, speckled trout and others, from flaky to firm. A fillet is usually sautéed: a wide pan and a little fat hot before it goes in, the presentation side down first, left alone to colour, turned once and finished gently. Many kitchens dust it with flour first, the meunière way, for a golden crust. Thin fillets take 2 to 3 minutes in all, most of it on the first side; thick ones finish in the oven. FDA guidance cooks fish to 63°C (145°F), opaque and flaking. Our kitchen's preparation is learned at lineup.

Lump crab is the large, sweet body meat of the blue crab, sold already cooked, so it is only warmed, in a little butter or under the salamander, the kitchen's overhead grill; cooked again it turns stringy and loses its sweetness. Pecans toast quickly: spread on a tray in an oven at about 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes, stirred once, until fragrant and a shade darker. A minute more and they turn bitter.

A New Orleans bordelaise is garlic and parsley in butter, often with olive oil, spooned hot over fish or bread; a pecan version works toasted pecans into it. The French bordelaise is another sauce entirely: red wine and shallot reduced with demi-glace, brown sauce reduced until glossy, and finished with bone marrow. A cauliflower purée is usually simmered in milk and cream and blended until velvety, lighter than potato, and collards wilted quickly keep a little chew.

New Orleans cooks have long put the pecan where French recipes put the almond. The praline became a pecan sweet, and fish à la meunière with almonds, amandine, found Louisiana cousins in pecan butter sauces and pecan-crusted fillets on menus across the city. The pecan is native to Louisiana and the Mississippi valley, rich, buttery and softer than an almond, which is why it melts so readily into a butter sauce.

This plate fails on timing. A pan not hot enough sticks and steams instead of colouring the fish, and a fillet left too long dries and falls apart. Lump crab cooked twice turns stringy, pecans a minute too long turn bitter, and garlic browned in butter held too hot turns acrid. A loose purée weeps water across the plate: cook it down.

On our plate the fish is the Gulf fish of the day, likely sautéed or pan-roasted to order, so know it and its preparation before service: every table will ask. The crab is Louisiana lump crab, warmed gently. The pecan bordelaise most likely belongs to the New Orleans garlic butter family, with toasted pecans worked into the butter, but that is a reading, not a recipe: confirm with the kitchen which bordelaise it is before pairing wine. Beneath sit the cauliflower purée and wilted collards, not the long-simmered Southern pot.

Offer it to a guest who wants fish at midday, something lighter than eggs, or the local catch: name today's fish first, then the crab. Do not confuse it with the Gulf Fish en Papillote at dinner, steamed in a banana leaf. This one plate carries fish, crab, pecans and very likely butter, so every allergen question, tree nuts and shellfish above all, goes to the service note and the kitchen before the order is placed. With a garlic butter bordelaise, a creamy, fresh Chardonnay suits; if today's sauce is red wine based, a light red Burgundy takes its place.

cards.back: The Gulf fish of the day topped with Louisiana lump crab, a pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens.

cards.front: What does Gulf fish mean on our menu?
cards.back: The day's catch, not one species: drum, sheepshead, snapper, trout and others. Learn today's fish and preparation at lineup.

cards.front: What are the two sauces called bordelaise?
cards.back: The French one is red wine and shallot reduced with demi-glace and bone marrow; in New Orleans it usually means garlic butter.

cards.front: Why confirm the bordelaise with the kitchen before pairing wine?
cards.back: A garlic butter calls for a creamy white such as Chardonnay; a red wine sauce calls for a light red, so the sauce decides the bottle.

cards.front: How is lump crab handled on the plate?
cards.back: It is already cooked, so it is only warmed gently; cooked again, it turns stringy and loses its sweetness.

cards.front: How is a fish fillet sautéed?
cards.back: In a little hot fat in a wide pan, presentation side first, left to colour, turned once and finished gently, in the oven if thick.

cards.front: How are pecans toasted, and what is the risk?
cards.back: In an oven at about 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes, stirred once; a minute too long and they turn bitter.

cards.front: Why do pecans dress fish in New Orleans?
cards.back: Louisiana cooks put the native pecan where French recipes used almonds, so amandine has pecan cousins: pecan butter sauces and pecan-crusted fish.

cards.back: Fish, crab, pecans and very likely butter: tree nut and shellfish questions go to the service note and the kitchen before ordering.

cards.front: How is the Pecan Gulf Fish told apart from the Gulf Fish en Papillote?
cards.back: The pecan fish is the breakfast and lunch plate, with a pecan bordelaise; the papillote is the dinner fish steamed in a banana leaf with olives and sorghum. Both carry crab and nuts, so send every allergen question to the kitchen.

cards.front: How do our collard greens differ from the Southern pot?
cards.back: They are wilted quickly and keep a little chew, not the long-simmered Southern pot; how they are seasoned is a question for the kitchen.

cards.front: When is a sautéed fillet done?
cards.back: At 63°C (145°F), when the flesh turns opaque and flakes at a touch; much past that it dries.

entries.title: The Chateaubriand with Foyot
entries.summary: The thick centre of the beef tenderloin, roasted whole and carved for two, with sauce Foyot, a béarnaise deepened with meat glaze. The cut brings tenderness; the sauce brings the depth the mild meat lacks.
entries.guest: The Chateaubriand serves two: the thick centre of a Creekstone Farms tenderloin, roasted whole, with glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, a béarnaise made richer with a reduced meat glaze.

paras: A Chateaubriand is the thick centre of the beef tenderloin, the long, slender muscle under the spine that does almost no work. Because it barely moves, it is the tenderest meat on the animal and also the mildest, with little fat running through it. The centre is the even, round stretch between the tapering tail and the knobbly head, so it roasts evenly and carves into neat slices. Cooked whole, it feeds two: a celebration plate, roasted, rested and carved for the table.

Sauce Foyot (fwah-YO) does the other half of the work: béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, with glace de viande, meat glaze, whisked in. The glaze, brown stock reduced until thick and syrupy, turns a pale, sharp béarnaise tawny and savoury, which is exactly what the mildest cut lacks. Making the sauce, and the story of its name, belong to Choron and Foyot.

The name honours François-René de Chateaubriand, the French writer and diplomat. Tradition credits his chef, Montmireil, with the dish around 1822; tell it as a story. Butchers define the cut in different ways: in France it is usually a thick steak from the heart of the fillet, the British name for the tenderloin; some older books take it from the head end; and in America it often means the whole centre-cut roast for two.

A Chateaubriand for two weighs roughly 450 to 680 g (16 to 24 oz) trimmed. Strip off the silverskin, the tough, shiny membrane that never softens, and tie the meat at 2.5 cm (1 inch) intervals so it holds an even round. Salt it well, sear it on every side in a hot pan for 6 to 8 minutes until deep brown, then roast it at about 200°C (392°F) for 15 to 25 minutes, checking the centre with a probe thermometer.

Pull it before the finish, because stored heat carries on into the centre as it rests: about 51°C (124°F) for a medium-rare finish near 55°C (131°F). Rest it on a rack, loosely covered, for about 10 minutes; the theory belongs to Roast and baste. Then remove the string and carve across the grain, which in a tenderloin runs the length of the muscle, into slices about 2 cm (3/4 inch) thick. Sauce at the last moment: Foyot is a warm emulsion, and a scorching plate splits it.

One roast comes to one temperature, so doneness is agreed once, with both guests. The ends are always a little more done than the centre, but sending the ends to one guest and the centre to the other is the kitchen's decision, never the server's promise.

A grey band under the crust means too much heat for too long. Done at one end and raw at the other means the meat was not tied, or came from the tail. Juice on the board means it had no rest; chewy edges mean silverskin left on.

At Brennan's the Roasted Chateaubriand is on the dinner menu: Creekstone Farms beef tenderloin, roasted whole, with roasted and glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, printed to serve two. Creekstone Farms is a Black Angus producer in Arkansas City, Kansas; never call this tenderloin Prime unless the kitchen confirms it.

The squash are young summer kinds, such as courgette, yellow squash and pattypan, roasted until their edges brown and glossed with a glaze, usually butter with a little stock or honey: a light, seasonal partner that changes with the market. Whether the roast is carved at the table or in the kitchen, and tonight's cooking time, are lineup questions.

Offer it early, to a couple celebrating or two guests who both want beef, because a whole roast takes longer than a steak; confirm the timing with the kitchen and tell the table honestly. Say plainly that it serves two, ask the temperature once and write it on the ticket. Describe it simply: the centre of the tenderloin, very tender and mild, roasted whole, with béarnaise made richer with a reduced beef glaze. The house guide suggests a shared side, Maggie's Mushrooms or the Shells & Cheese; questions about the sauce go to the kitchen.

entries.title: The hanger steak with béarnaise
entries.summary: Brennan's breakfast steak and eggs: a Creole-spiced Creekstone Prime hanger, cooked hot and fast, sliced across the grain and served with French béarnaise, a smoked potato pavé and a sunny-side-up egg. The same cut returns at dinner on different foundations.
entries.guest: Our Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is Creekstone Prime hanger with a smoked potato pavé, a sunny-side-up Vital Farms egg and classic French béarnaise. How would you like it cooked?

paras: The hanger is the butcher's steak. It hangs from the diaphragm, the sheet of muscle under the ribs that works with every breath, close to the kidneys. There is only one on each animal, so butchers often kept it for themselves, and in France it is the onglet of the bistro. A tough sinew runs down its middle and is cut out, leaving two long lobes with a loose, coarse grain. It tastes deeply beefy, with a rich, mineral edge, and it rewards hot, fast cooking.

On this plate two traditions meet. Béarnaise (bair-NAYZ), hollandaise built on a reduction of vinegar, shallot and tarragon, is the classic French sauce for beef: its sharpness cuts the richness and its herbs lift the meat. Creole spice seasons the steak itself: a blend usually built on paprika, cayenne and black pepper, though the house's own blend is not printed, so spice questions go to the kitchen. A French plate with a New Orleans accent.

Trim any membrane left on the outside and check the central sinew is gone; a whole hanger is usually split into its two lobes, each about 4 cm (1 1/2 inches) thick. Season it well with salt and the Creole spice. Sear it in a very hot pan or on a hot grill, turning it every minute or so, for about 8 to 12 minutes in all, until the crust is deep brown; for medium rare, pull it at about 52 to 54°C (126 to 129°F), and it climbs a little as it rests.

Rest it for 5 minutes, then slice it across the grain. The hanger's fibres are long and slant across each lobe, so look before you cut and turn the knife until it crosses them. Slices about 1 cm (3/8 inch) thick, cut on a slight angle, eat tenderly; cut along the grain and the same steak chews like string. Add the béarnaise last, on warm meat, never straight from a scorching pan.

The hanger is tender only while it is pink. Its coarse fibres are bundled in sheaths of connective tissue. As the meat passes about 60°C (140°F), the fibre proteins tighten and squeeze out their juice, and the collagen in the sheaths shrinks and pulls the bundles tighter still. A hanger then turns dry and stringy, and its rich flavour turns to liver. Most kitchens recommend medium rare to medium and treat medium as the limit, and the choice stays with the guest.
Other faults are simpler: a pale crust means a wet steak or a pan not hot enough, a gristly bite is the sinew left in, and juice flooding the plate means it had no rest.

The same cut stands on different foundations at dinner. The Creole Hanger Steak carries housemade Creole spice with chilli crisp, a crunchy Chinese chilli oil with real heat, a pepita persillade and Madeira-glazed broccolini, and no egg and no béarnaise. The breakfast plate leans French, sauce and potato; the dinner plate leans on heat and crunch. The dinner plate's persillade and its build belong to The menu read by method.

At Brennan's the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is a breakfast and lunch main course: Creekstone Farms Prime hanger, a smoked potato pavé, a sunny-side-up Vital Farms egg and French béarnaise. The pavé (pah-VAY) is potato sliced paper thin, layered with cream and butter, baked, pressed overnight, cut into bricks and seared crisp; how the smoke gets in is the kitchen's detail. Vital Farms eggs are pasture raised, each hen with at least 10 square metres (108 square feet) of rotated pasture. The house guide puts the hanger at its best medium rare to medium; the menu prints both supplier names, and lineup, the short staff meeting before each service, confirms they are still current before you say them.

Take the temperature as you take the order and write it on the ticket. If a guest is unsure, say the hanger is most tender pink, but the choice is theirs. Say it plainly: steak and eggs done properly, a beefy butcher's cut with Creole spice, crisp layered potato, a runny yolk and the classic steak sauce. Keep the two hangers apart: breakfast has béarnaise and an egg, dinner has chilli crisp and neither. Questions about what is in the spice or the sauce go to the kitchen.

entries.title: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits.
entries.summary: Brennan's Creole answer to a Lowcountry breakfast: Louisiana shrimp in a tomato Creole sauce seasoned with tasso, over a fried pimento cheese grit cake, with fried okra chips. Creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, built on the trinity.
entries.guest: Our Shrimp & Grits puts Louisiana shrimp in a Creole sauce with tasso over a fried pimento cheese grit cake, crisp outside and creamy inside, with crunchy okra chips.

paras: Shrimp and grits is a Southern coastal breakfast; Brennan's plate is its New Orleans version. Louisiana shrimp are cooked in Creole sauce, the city's tomato sauce built on the trinity, with tasso (TAH-so), a spiced, smoked pork, cooked into it. Under them is not a bowl of soft grits but a grit cake: grits made with pimento cheese, set firm, cut and fried until crisp outside and creamy within. Fried okra chips go on top for crunch. Learn it by its contrasts: creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy.

The dish began in the South Carolina Lowcountry, the coast around Charleston, as breakfast shrimp: fresh shrimp cooked in butter or bacon fat and eaten over grits. Charleston recipes for it were in print by 1930. In 1985 Craig Claiborne wrote up Bill Neal's version from Crook's Corner in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, with bacon, lemon and cheese grits, in The New York Times, and it went national.

The old Charleston recipes dress the shrimp in butter; Bill Neal's Chapel Hill version uses bacon fat and lemon. The New Orleans plate swaps both for a tomato Creole sauce on the trinity, with tasso for smoke.

Grits are ground dried maize; some products are made from hominy and others are not. Grain type and grind affect liquid needs and cooking time. A general grit-cake method cooks grits until hydrated, spreads the mixture in a shallow tray, cools it under an appropriate controlled process and cuts it once firm. This explains the structure; the kitchen's current formula determines the pimento cheese, proportions, thickness and production schedule.

For a general fried grit cake, coating, oil temperature and time follow the chosen recipe. Fry manageable batches, drain as directed and check the intended crisp surface and heated centre. Brennan's saved menu specifies a fried pimento cheese grit cake and fried okra chips, but it does not establish the coating, fryer arrangement or production timing. Confirm those details with the kitchen.

The Creole sauce begins with the trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, softened in fat, with diced tasso browned first in a little fat so its smoke and spice flavour the pan; tomato, stock and herbs then simmer into a coating sauce. Creole sauce, Tasso and Okra each have their own entry. Shrimp readiness is checked against the verified cooking process and an appropriate thermometer. Pearly, opaque flesh is a useful sensory observation; colour, elapsed minutes or a C-shaped curl alone do not establish the endpoint.

A cake that falls apart was cooked too loose or chilled too briefly; a greasy one met oil that was too cool, often from crowding the pan. Rubbery shrimp cooked too long, slimy okra was cut thick or fried slowly, and a soggy cake sat under its sauce too long: fry the cake to order and spoon the shrimp and sauce over it at the pass, the counter where the kitchen finishes plates and hands them to the servers.

At Brennan's the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits is a breakfast and lunch main course: Louisiana shrimp, a fried pimento cheese grit cake, tasso, Creole sauce and fried okra chips. Pimento cheese is grated sharp cheddar bound with mayonnaise and sweet red pimientos; folded into the grits before they set, it makes the cake tangy and creamy inside. Louisiana is one of the country's largest shrimp producers, so the word on the menu is worth saying. Whether the tasso is smoked in house, and whether tonight's shrimp are brown or white, are questions for the kitchen. The house guide gives TAH-so; TASS-oh is also heard, and the house habit is a question for lineup, the short staff meeting before each service.

Tell the guest it comes as a fried cake, so nobody expects a creamy bowl. Describe it the house way: creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, with mild to moderate spice from the tasso and the sauce. It suits a guest who wants something savoury and Southern, or someone trying grits for the first time. When a guest asks about shellfish, pork, cheese or fried coatings, read the service note and take the question to the kitchen.

entries.title: Bananas Foster at the table
entries.say: As it reads: Bananas Foster at the table.
entries.summary: Brennan's signature dessert, created in 1951 and flamed at the guéridon: bananas in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, banana liqueur and burning rum, spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream. The story, the service and the words to say.
entries.guest: Bananas Foster was created at Brennan's in 1951. We cook bananas in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, flame them with rum at your table and spoon them over our vanilla ice cream.

paras: Bananas Foster is the dessert Brennan's gave the world, and here it is made in front of the guest. On a guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), the tableside cart, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melt into a caramel, the bananas soften in it, rum is set alight, and all of it is spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream, hot over cold. It is cooked in one pan for at least two, which is why it is ordered in twos. The house calls it the most ordered dish on the menu; whether to say so at the table is a question for lineup, the short staff meeting before each service.

It was created in 1951, while the restaurant was still Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré on Bourbon Street, five years before the move to 417 Royal Street. Owen asked for a new dessert for a dinner honouring his friend Richard Foster of the New Orleans Crime Commission. His sister Ella Brennan and the chef Paul Blangé (blahn-ZHAY) adapted a family dish, the caramelised bananas their mother made at home, and named it for Foster.

That is the telling on the house's own Traditions and recipe pages; the server guide tells it as Owen's challenge to Blangé. Which telling to use, and which name for the commission (it is also called the Metropolitan Crime Commission), are a manager's call at lineup.
Bananas made sense. New Orleans was then the great port of entry for bananas from Central and South America. 2026 is the dessert's 75th year.

The kitchen build belongs to Bananas Foster; at the table, learn the order, because the guest watches every step. The cart is set where nothing hangs overhead, with the spirits measured into small vessels beforehand.

Butter and brown sugar melt and bubble into a smooth, blond caramel, dusted with cinnamon. Banana liqueur goes in, as the house's published recipe has it. The bananas, ripe but firm, halved and quartered, are laid in and turned once so they soften without collapsing. The pan comes off the flame, the measured rum goes in, and back on the flame the pan is tilted so the far edge catches, away from the guests. As it burns, the caramel deepens; when the flame has died, the bananas go over the ice cream and the warm sauce follows.

The menu prints rum; the published recipe adds banana liqueur. Follow the cart build confirmed at lineup, and never quote quantities. The flame rules belong to Flambé safety, learned word for word; a new server never lights a pan before sign off.

Bananas that collapse were too ripe or stewed too long. A sauce that sets hard on the ice cream was taken past blond into toffee. Ice cream melted to soup was scooped too early. In a bright room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it has clearly died. A guest leaning in is too close: seat everyone back before the rum goes in.

World Famous Bananas Foster is printed at breakfast, lunch and dinner, and it closes the Traditional Breakfast tasting, with Congregation Coffee & Chicory. The menu prints it flambéed tableside, with a minimum of two per order; whether the printed price is per person or per order is a lineup question, so never quote it until a manager says. The ice cream is made in house, and questions about what goes into it go to the kitchen. Who performs the flambé is a question for the manager.

Seed it with the main course order, so the cart is ready when the table is: every first visit, every celebration, every guest who asks what Brennan's is famous for. Remind the table it is made for two or more. Pour any wine before the flambé starts, so no glass sits near the flame.

Tell the story while the caramel bubbles: created at Brennan's in 1951, named for Richard Foster. Then the cue, "Now the rum, please sit back just a little", and stop talking. Let the flame have the room. When it has died, one line as you plate: over our vanilla ice cream, then the warm sauce.

Be exact about alcohol: flaming burns the vapour above the pan, and alcohol can remain in the sauce. Tell any guest who avoids alcohol before they order, and ask the kitchen to verify an alternative from its current recipe and products.

entries.title: Breakfast at Brennan's
entries.say: As it reads: Breakfast at Brennan's.
entries.summary: Breakfast at Brennan's is the house's defining idea: a long, celebratory morning meal of an eye opener, a soup, an egg dish and a flamed dessert. Learn its shape, the plates on their foundations and how to sell the morning.
entries.guest: Breakfast here is a celebration rather than a quick bite: a morning cocktail, a soup, one of our egg dishes and Bananas Foster flamed at your table. The Traditional Breakfast brings you all of it.

paras: Breakfast at Brennan's is not a dish but a shape: a long, celebratory morning meal taken in courses, the way most restaurants serve dinner. It is the idea the house is known for, and still the reason many guests come to 417 Royal Street. A server who understands the shape can guide any table, whether the guest wants one plate or the whole ritual.

The shape has four parts: an eye opener, which is a morning cocktail; a soup; an egg dish; and a dessert flamed at the table. Everything else on the breakfast menu, the sweet starters, the omelette, the waffle and the sides, fits around those four.

Owen Brennan noticed that most New Orleans restaurants served only lunch and dinner. He took his cue from Dinner at Antoine's, Frances Parkinson Keyes's popular 1948 novel, and asked why not Breakfast at Brennan's. He made the morning an occasion: something to wake the palate, something warm, the egg dishes the house became known for, and a flame to finish. His story, and his sister Ella's, has its own entry.
The idea outlived him. Bananas Foster, created at Brennan's in 1951, became the flame that ends the meal. Breakfast and lunch now runs from 9 to 2 on weekdays and from 8 to 2 at weekends.

The Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's walks a guest through the whole ritual, with tasting portions of each course and every listed drink in the one price. It opens with the eye opener, a Brandy Milk Punch of brandy, cream, vanilla and nutmeg. A baked apple with an oat and pecan crumble follows, then turtle soup or seafood gumbo with a Bloody Bull, a Bloody Mary made with beef bouillon.

Next come the Eggs Hussarde with 120 ml (4 oz) of Champagne, a petite filet mignon with 120 ml (4 oz) of Côtes du Rhône, and Bananas Foster flamed at the table with chicory coffee. That is roughly four drinks in a morning, so offer a spirit-free drink in place of any pour without being asked; the price does not change. Read the printed card on shift, since courses and pours can change.

The other plates stand on classical foundations. The Framboise French Toast is pain perdu, lost bread: housemade citrus brioche soaked in custard and fried, classically in butter. The Crab & Corn Omelette starts from the omelette, eggs cooked fast in a buttered pan; whether it is rolled the French way or folded is a question for lineup, the short staff meeting before each service. The Duck Confit Waffle carries a Rohan duck leg cooked slowly in fat, which is confit, then crisped. The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake borrows the flavours of the flaming spiced coffee without the flame.

The sides round out an egg dish: Brabant potatoes (bra-BAHNT), cubes fried crisp and, in the old Creole way, tossed in butter, garlic and parsley, with the house finish confirmed at lineup; creamed spinach, squeezed dry and bound with cream; Cheddar Grits; and an Egg Any Style. Children ten and under have their own breakfast at one set price covering fruit, the plate, ice cream and a drink: eggs any style with toast and bacon, vanilla French toast with berries, popcorn shrimp or a grilled cheese, the last two with Brabant potatoes.

Sell the morning as a sequence, not a single plate. A first-time table hears the classic in one breath: a Brandy Milk Punch, the turtle soup, the Eggs Hussarde and Bananas Foster at the table, with the Traditional Breakfast as the easy yes if they want all of it. Seed the Foster as the main courses are ordered, since it is made for two or more. Then pace it: drinks first, soup while the kitchen cooks the eggs, the cart once plates are cleared.

Write every egg style exactly as the guest says it. Questions about what is in a dish, an allergy or a diet go to the kitchen every time: the breakfast is built on eggs, butter and cream, so never guess at a plate.

brennans.how: The Framboise French Toast is pain perdu made with housemade citrus brioche, mascarpone mousse, raspberry coulis and local raspberries; it sits among the starters, so offer it for the table to share before the egg dishes.

The Crab & Corn Omelette is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata; ask at lineup whether it is rolled French style or folded.

The Rohan duck leg is confit, cooked slowly in fat and crisped, on a cornbread and chive waffle with foie gras butter, mustard maple syrup and a sunny-side-up egg. Describe the method, and promise no house times.

The coffee cake borrows the flaming coffee's flavours: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. The drink itself is not on our list, so sell the flavours, not the flame.
Brabant potatoes are a breakfast side: cubed potatoes fried golden and crisp, then tossed in butter with garlic and parsley in the old Creole way. Confirm the house finish and the fryer at lineup.
Creamed spinach is a breakfast and lunch side, spinach squeezed dry and bound with cream; whether it is the same preparation as the Parmesan spinach under the Sardou is a question for the kitchen.
Cheddar Grits are coarse-ground corn simmered slowly until creamy and finished with cheddar; whether they are stone-ground, and whose corn, are questions for the kitchen.
An Egg Any Style is one egg cooked as the guest asks: sunny side up, over easy, medium or hard, scrambled or soft-boiled. Write the style exactly, and confirm the styles offered at lineup.
The children's eggs any style come with toast and bacon; ask the parent how the child likes them and write the style on the ticket word for word.
The children's vanilla French toast is the same lost bread idea in a plainer form, with fresh berries and whipped cream, inside the one set price for children ten and under.
On the children's breakfast the popcorn shrimp come with Brabant potatoes, the crisp cubed potatoes of the old Creole dining rooms.
The children's grilled cheese sandwich is served with Brabant potatoes, so a child gets the same crisp New Orleans side as the grown-ups.

Start them on the Foster alone

entries.title: Flambé and tableside service
entries.summary: Tableside service brings the last of the cooking into the dining room, on a cart called a guéridon. Learn where it comes from, the flamed desserts it carries at Brennan's, the choreography at the cart and why New Orleans kept it.
entries.guest: Dessert here can be finished right beside your table: Bananas Foster is cooked on the cart, flamed with rum and spooned over our vanilla ice cream.

paras: Tableside service is cooking, carving or finishing a dish in the dining room, in front of the guest. It is done on a guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), a small wheeled table or cart that carries a burner, a pan and everything the dish needs. Flambé (flahm-BAY) means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so the alcohol vapour burns above the sauce in a short burst of flame.

It matters because it is the moment many guests remember from Brennan's, and because it turns a server into a cook in full view. Done well, it is theatre and flavour at once; done carelessly, it is a fire in a full room.

The guéridon belongs to the grand dining rooms of Europe, where a maître d'hôtel, the head waiter, or a captain, the senior server who runs a section, carved, dressed and flamed beside the table. American hotel schools call this French service, although in France the old service à la française meant every dish of a course set on the table at once. That gave way in the nineteenth century to service à la russe, courses brought in order, and the cart became the stage for the last touch.

Cherries Jubilee is the old flamed classic. It is generally credited to Auguste Escoffier for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be the Diamond Jubilee of 1897, though some accounts give the Golden Jubilee of 1887. His version was poached cherries in a thickened syrup with warmed kirsch, a cherry brandy, lit at the table, and no ice cream; the ice cream came later, largely in America.

Across most of America, tableside cooking faded in the later twentieth century as plates came to be finished in the kitchen. One reason often given for its survival here is that the old New Orleans houses kept career waiters and captains, rooms built for occasion and dishes whose whole point is the flame, and visitors came looking for exactly that.

Cherries Jubilee is the eldest of a small family. Crêpes Suzette, thin pancakes flamed in an orange butter sauce, come from the same European rooms. Café brûlot is the New Orleans cousin: brandy and orange liqueur flamed with spices and citrus peel, then ladled into strong coffee, a ritual Antoine's credits to Jules Alciatore. Bananas Foster is the Brennan's signature. Each has its own entry.

The choreography is learned before the first flame. The cart is set first: burner checked, pan, the spirit already measured into a small vessel, a lid, the plates, and ice cream timed to arrive cold. It stands where nothing hangs overhead, away from drapes and air vents, with menus and napkins cleared, and the guests stay seated and back from it. In many rooms one person cooks and flames while a second serves, so the dessert lands while the ice cream still holds its shape; at Brennan's, who does what is a question for the manager.

The spirit goes in only with the pan pulled off the flame, never from the bottle and never into a pan already alight; the far edge is tilted to the burner so the flame rises away from cook and guests. Let it burn out before plating, and turn the burner off before leaving the cart. Flaming burns the vapour, not all the alcohol; alcohol can remain in the sauce. Flambé safety in full has its own entry.

Bananas Foster is the house signature: bananas in a blond, bubbling caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, flamed with rum and spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream, made in one pan for two or more. Cherries Jubilee, fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce flamed over the same ice cream, is not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026, so confirm with a manager before offering it. Who performs the flambé, and the sign-off before a new server lights a pan, are questions for training.

Read the room before the cart rolls: an anniversary table wants a hushed show, a birthday table the whole story. Tell the story before the flame, while the caramel bubbles: 1951, named for Richard Foster, in the house's telling once a manager has confirmed it. Then go quiet: the pan needs your full attention, and the flame is the line. In a bright morning room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it has clearly died down.

faults.cause: The caramel was too cool, or the rum had no time to warm and give off vapour.
faults.fix: Bring the caramel to a full bubble first and let the rum warm in the pan for a few seconds before tilting it to the flame; never add more spirit to a pan that may already be alight.

faults.cause: Too much spirit, or spirit poured from the bottle.
faults.fix: Measure into a small vessel beforehand and keep a lid within reach to smother the pan.

faults.fault: A flame that reaches something overhead
faults.cause: The cart was set under a vent, drape or low décor.
faults.fix: Set the cart where nothing hangs overhead, away from drapes and air vents, before the burner is lit.

faults.fault: A guest too close to the pan
faults.cause: Guests leaning in, or a child, loose sleeve or long hair near the cart.
faults.fix: Seat everyone back from the cart before the spirit goes in.

faults.fault: The ice cream melts before it reaches the guest
faults.cause: Scooped too early, or one person cooking and serving alone.
faults.fix: Time the ice cream to the flame, with a second pair of hands if the house works that way.

brennans.how: Bananas Foster is made on the guéridon: butter, brown sugar and cinnamon taken to a blond caramel, bananas turned once, rum added off the flame and lit, then spooned over vanilla ice cream, for two or more.

Fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce are flamed at the table over housemade vanilla ice cream. It is off the 3 October 2026 dessert menu, so confirm with a manager; ask the chef which spirit is lit and whether the cherries are pitted.

cards.front: Why do many rooms have one person flame and another serve?

cards.front: How do you read the room and time your words at the cart?
cards.back: Read the room first: a hushed show for an anniversary, the whole story for a birthday. Tell the story before the flame, while the caramel bubbles; go quiet as the rum goes in, eyes on the pan, guests seated and back.

cards.front: Why did tableside cooking last in New Orleans?
cards.back: The reasons often given: the old houses kept career waiters and captains, rooms built for occasion and dishes whose point is the flame, and visitors came for exactly that.

cards.front: Why treat the pan as lit in a bright breakfast room?
