questions.q: In tableside service, what is a guéridon?
questions.answer: A wheeled cart with a burner beside the table
distractors: A long-handled lighter for igniting the spirit
The captain's station by the door
questions.why: The guéridon is the cart that carries the burner, the pan and everything prepared for the dish, so the last of the cooking happens in view of the guest.

questions.q: The rum goes into a pan of cool caramel and will not catch. Why?
questions.answer: Too little alcohol vapour rises to burn
distractors: The sugar has not yet caramelised
The butter in the caramel smothers the flame
Rum burns only in a copper pan
questions.why: Only the alcohol vapour burns, and a cool pan gives off too little of it: bring the caramel to a full bubble and let the rum warm a few seconds, never adding more spirit.

questions.q: Escoffier's Cherries Jubilee: which spirit was lit, and was it served with ice cream?
questions.answer: Warmed kirsch, and no ice cream
distractors: Dark rum, over vanilla ice cream
questions.why: His version was poached cherries in a thickened syrup lit with warm kirsch; the ice cream is a later, largely American habit.

questions.q: A guest asks for Cherries Jubilee. What do you do first?
questions.answer: Confirm with a manager that it is served
distractors: Fire it straight away with the Foster
Tell the guest it was retired years ago
Offer to flame it with a spirit of their choice
questions.why: It is not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026, so a manager confirms it before it is offered or promised.

questions.q: Which service style brought courses to the table one after another?
questions.answer: Service à la russe
questions.why: Service à la russe brought courses in order and replaced service à la française, where every dish of a course was set out at once; the cart kept the last touch.

questions.q: When is the rum added to the Bananas Foster pan?
questions.answer: Off the flame, from a measured vessel
distractors: Straight from the bottle over the burner
Into the pan once it is already alight
Before the butter and sugar go in
questions.why: Measured spirit, added with the pan pulled away from the flame, keeps the bottle and the cook's hand away from a burst of fire.

questions.q: An anniversary couple at a quiet corner table orders the Foster. How does reading the room shape the service?
questions.answer: A hushed show, the story kept short
distractors: The full story, told for the whole room
No flame, plated in the kitchen instead
The next table invited over to watch
questions.why: Reading the room comes before the cart rolls: an anniversary wants a hushed show, a birthday the whole story. Either way the story comes before the flame, and quiet during it.

questions.q: Tableside cooking faded across most of America. Which reason is often given for its survival in the old New Orleans dining rooms?
questions.answer: They kept career waiters and captains
distractors: A city ordinance required flamed desserts
Rum was cheaper at the port
Their kitchens were too small for desserts
questions.why: The reasons often given: the old houses kept career waiters and captains, rooms built for occasion and dishes whose point is the flame, and visitors came looking for exactly that.

questions.q: Which flamed New Orleans ritual is the coffee cousin of Bananas Foster?
questions.answer: Café brûlot
questions.why: Café brûlot flames brandy and orange liqueur with spices and citrus peel, then ladles it into strong coffee at the table.

entries.title: The menu read by method
entries.say: As it reads: the menu read by method.
entries.summary: The Brennan's menu read by method rather than by dish: steam in a leaf, a blackening pan, the fryer, slow fat, the roasting pan, the rice pot, and the pastry kitchen's custards, caramel and laminated dough. A map from technique to plate.
entries.guest: Our kitchen cooks each plate its own way: the Gulf fish steams in a banana leaf, the poussin is brined in sweet tea and fried, and the tasting's duck breast is roasted crisp.

paras: A menu read by method is a menu you can explain without memorising it. Every plate is a technique applied to an ingredient, and the technique tells you the texture, the timing and the honest words for the guest.

Ask four questions of any plate. What is the cooking medium: steam, dry heat, hot fat, or none at all? How hot, and for how long? What does that do to texture: moist, crusted, crisp or silky? And what does it mean for the ticket: a cooking time, a doneness to ask, a raw food advisory?

Steam and fierce heat. The Gulf Fish en Papillote is the classical parcel in banana leaf instead of paper, sealed and baked, classically in a hot oven around 205°C (400°F) for 10 to 15 minutes, so the fish steams in its own juices, here with crab, sorghum, olives, tomato and Marcona almonds. The Blackened Tofu takes Paul Prudhomme's method from K-Paul's, around 1980, onto local tofu: a spice crust charred dark in a minute or two a side in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking. Prudhomme dipped his fish in butter first, so ask the kitchen before anyone says vegan.

Fat, fast and slow. The Poussin à la Moutarde is a Cornish hen soaked in a sweet tea brine of strong black tea, sugar and salt, coated and fried until the skin is crisp and the thickest part of the thigh reads 74°C (165°F), then sauced with a Burgundian mustard cream, the mustard stirred in off the heat so it keeps its bite; how long it brines and how it is fried are chef questions. The Rohan (ROH-han) duck leg is confit, cooked slowly under fat and crisped for the Duck Confit Waffle: describe the method, and promise no house times.

The roasting pan and the spice shelf. The Rohan breast is scored and started skin down in a cold or moderate pan so its fat renders slowly and the skin crisps, then finished in the oven, rested and sliced pink, with cane syrup-glazed peaches. The Creole Hanger Steak carries the housemade Creole spice, a pepita persillade of parsley, garlic and toasted pumpkin seeds, and Madeira-glazed broccolini. South Louisiana Rice Dressing folds rice into seasoned minced meat browned with the trinity, often bound with a little roux or gravy, cousin to dirty rice.

The pastry kitchen. The New Orleans Bread Pudding is bread baked in custard, under a whiskey caramel. The Snickers is a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, crème anglaise usually set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, with a caramel custard; for a guest who avoids gelatine, the kitchen confirms. The Lemon Tart wears a cooked meringue, Italian or Swiss, toasted with a torch. The Pineapple Tarte Tatin is the upside-down tart: classically the fruit is caramelised in butter and sugar in the pan, covered with puff pastry, baked and turned out so the pastry sits beneath. The puff pastry is laminated, raised by steam from its butter; the sweetened condensed anglaise is a pouring custard, never boiled.

Smaller touches carry methods too: steak tartare, seasoned raw beef, in the fried potato cannoli; brown butter in the financiers of the Blackberry Trifle; the raw Creole tomatoes of the tostada, where the method is restraint; and the children's Gulf fish, simply sautéed and turned once.

Each method has a fault you can learn to see. A papillote left too long dries the fish inside a scorched leaf. A blackening pan held too long turns the crust acrid. Oil that is too cool gives pale, greasy skin. A duck breast started too hot keeps a band of unrendered fat. An anglaise pulled at about 82°C (180°F), when it coats the spoon, is right; taken much past 85°C (185°F) it curdles.

Lead with the method, then the flavour: baked in a banana leaf so it steams in its own juices; brined in sweet tea, fried and sauced with a French mustard cream. Methods also set the clock and the ticket. The parcel and the bone-in bird take far longer than a fillet, so both are fired ahead of the course; the kitchen's fire times are learned at lineup. The duck breast and the hanger need a doneness, and a pink duck breast sits below the Food Code's 74°C (165°F) for poultry, so like the tartare's raw beef it needs a consumer advisory; confirm the house wording at lineup. Allergy questions go to the kitchen.

ratios.label: The holy trinity
ratios.value: Onion, celery and green pepper, often 2 parts onion to 1 each of celery and pepper

ratios.label: Crème anglaise, a classic proportion
ratios.value: 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk to 8 to 10 yolks and 200 to 250 g (7 to 9 oz) of sugar

ratios.label: Brine for a small bird, a working guide
ratios.value: About 50 g (1 3/4 oz) of salt per 1 litre (about 1 quart) of sweet tea, a few hours; the house time is a question for the chef

ratios.label: Confit cure
ratios.value: Legs salted with garlic and herbs for 12 to 24 hours, rinsed, then 2.5 to 3 hours under fat at a bare tremble, about 90°C (194°F), until the meat yields at the bone and a skewer slides in freely

ratios.label: Bavarian cream
ratios.value: About 15 g (1/2 oz) of gelatine per 1 litre (about 1 quart) of anglaise, with about an equal volume of whipped cream

temps.label: A hot oven for a fish parcel, typically
Frying oil, a common working heat
Duck fat for confit, a bare tremble
Crème anglaise coats the spoon; never boil it
Poultry cooked to, thickest part (FDA Food Code)
Duck breast pulled for medium rare; the house standard is confirmed at lineup

faults.fault: Dry fish in a scorched leaf
faults.cause: The papillote was left in too long or the oven ran too hot.
faults.fix: Time the parcel to the thickness of the fillet and pull it while the fish just flakes.

faults.cause: The spice sat too long in a pan heated past smoking.
faults.fix: About 2 minutes a side over the highest heat, under a strong extractor, until the underside looks charred; the crust should be dark, never burnt.

faults.cause: Oil too cool, or the basket overloaded.
faults.fix: Heat the oil to about 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F) before loading, fry in small batches, keep it near 160 to 165°C (320 to 329°F) for bone-in pieces and drain on a rack.

faults.fault: Flabby duck skin over a band of fat
faults.cause: The breast went into a pan too hot, so the fat never rendered.
faults.fix: Score it, start it skin down in a cold or moderate pan and render slowly before the turn.

faults.cause: It was boiled, and the yolks set into curds.
faults.fix: Stir gently to about 82°C (180°F), when it coats a spoon, and strain at once into a cold bowl.

brennans.how: The Gulf fish is wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper, with crab, sorghum, olives, tomato and Marcona almonds, so it steams in its own juices; ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn of the steam.

Prudhomme's blackening, a spice crust toasted dark in a very hot dry pan, is applied to New Orleans Tien Dat tofu; the classic method uses butter, so check with the kitchen before calling the dish vegan.

A Cornish hen brined in sweet tea, fried crisp and sauced with a Burgundian mustard cream, with turnips and shallots: Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce, which is the line to give the guest.

On the dinner tasting the Rohan breast is roasted with its fat rendered and its skin crisp, served pink, with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts; confirm the kitchen's doneness at lineup.
The Rohan duck leg on the breakfast Duck Confit Waffle is confit, cooked slowly in fat and then crisped; describe the method in general and promise no house times.

The Creekstone Farms hanger takes the housemade Creole spice, a pepita persillade of parsley, garlic and toasted pumpkin seed, and Madeira-glazed broccolini; the glaze is made with wine, worth saying to guests who avoid alcohol.
Rice folded into seasoned minced meat browned with the trinity, a dinner side with no description printed; it is cousin to dirty rice, so confirm the meats with the kitchen before describing it.
Bread pudding baked in custard and served with a whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines; the caramel carries whiskey, so tell guests who avoid alcohol.

The chocolate bar rebuilt: a milk chocolate Bavarian cream for the chocolate and a caramel custard for the caramel, with nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts; the house guide flags peanuts, so confirm with the kitchen for every table.
Toasted meringue sits with yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and a sweet pastry crumb, the French lemon tart taken apart; which meringue style the pastry kitchen uses is a question for the chef.

The upside-down tart made with charred pineapple instead of apple, on puff pastry, with a sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse; whether it is baked inverted or built on the plate is a question for the chef.
Seasoned raw beef is piped into a crisp potato cannoli shell with crème fraîche and grated cured egg yolk; it carries a raw beef advisory, so read the service note and send questions to the kitchen.

The blackberry financier biscuits in the trifle are made with brown butter, which gives them their nutty, buttery taste; financiers are traditionally made with almond flour, so confirm with the kitchen.
Louisiana heirloom and Creole tomatoes are served raw with burrata, an okra tostada and smoked tomato water; the dish follows the season, so expect it to change when the tomatoes finish.
The children's Gulf fish is sautéed: a hot pan, a little fat, left to colour, turned once and finished gently, served with potato and green beans; know today's fish at lineup.

FDA Food Code, US Food and Drug Administration

cards.front: What four questions read any plate by method?
cards.back: The cooking medium, the heat and time, what it does to texture, and what it means for the ticket: a time, a doneness or an advisory.

cards.front: How is the Gulf Fish en Papillote cooked?
cards.back: Sealed in a banana leaf rather than paper and baked, so the fish steams in its own juices with crab, olives, tomato and almonds.

cards.front: What is blackening, and who created it?
cards.back: A spice crust toasted dark in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking; Paul Prudhomme, at K-Paul's around 1980. Here it is on tofu.

cards.front: Which three methods meet on the Poussin à la Moutarde?
cards.back: A sweet tea brine, the fryer and a Burgundian mustard cream: Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce.

cards.front: How is the Rohan duck used twice on the menus?
cards.back: The breast is scored and started skin down in a cold or moderate pan to render its fat, then roasted and served pink on the dinner tasting; the leg is confit on the breakfast waffle.

cards.front: What is the pepita persillade on the Creole Hanger Steak, and what should a guest know about the broccolini?
cards.back: Persillade is parsley and garlic chopped fine and thrown on at the last second; pepitas are hulled pumpkin seeds toasted until they puff. The broccolini's glaze is Madeira reduced until syrupy, so tell guests who avoid alcohol.

cards.front: What is South Louisiana rice dressing?
cards.back: Rice folded into seasoned minced meat browned with the trinity, cousin to dirty rice; confirm the meats with the kitchen, since none are printed.

cards.front: What is the Bavarian cream in The Snickers?
cards.back: A crème anglaise, usually set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, here made with milk chocolate, beside a caramel custard. For a guest who avoids gelatine, ask the kitchen.

cards.front: Which foundations meet in the Pineapple Tarte Tatin?
cards.back: Caramel, puff pastry, a laminated dough raised by steam from its butter, and a sweetened condensed anglaise, a pouring custard.

cards.front: Why is a crème anglaise never boiled?
cards.back: Its yolks thicken it at about 82°C (180°F), when it coats a spoon; much hotter and they set into a grainy custard.

cards.front: Name the smaller touches on the menu read by method.
cards.back: Raw steak tartare in the fried potato cannoli, brown butter financiers in the Blackberry Trifle, raw Creole tomatoes on the tostada and the children's sautéed Gulf fish.

cards.front: Which plates set the clock or need a question on the ticket?
cards.back: The papillote and the whole poussin take time; the duck breast and the hanger need a doneness; the pink duck breast and the raw tartare carry an advisory.

questions.q: What wraps the Gulf Fish en Papillote at Brennan's?
questions.answer: A banana leaf
questions.why: The classical papillote is paper; here a banana leaf seals the parcel just as well, so the fish steams in its own juices.

questions.q: Who created the blackening method used on the Blackened Tofu?
questions.answer: Paul Prudhomme
questions.why: Prudhomme created blackening at K-Paul's around 1980; Alciatore is credited with pompano en papillote and Blangé with Bananas Foster.

questions.q: Which pairing is the whole idea of the Poussin à la Moutarde?
questions.answer: Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce
distractors: Roast chicken with a Creole tomato sauce
Grilled quail with a Burgundian red wine reduction
Poached hen with a classic hollandaise
questions.why: A sweet tea-brined, fried Cornish hen meets a Burgundian mustard cream, two traditions on one plate.

questions.q: How is the Rohan duck breast started, so its fat renders and the skin crisps?
questions.answer: Skin down in a cold or moderate pan
distractors: Skin up under a very hot grill
Plunged whole into hot frying oil
Poached in duck fat for hours
questions.why: Skin down in a cold or moderate pan melts the fat slowly as the skin crisps; started too hot, a band of fat stays. The leg, not the breast, is the confit.

questions.q: Before describing the South Louisiana Rice Dressing, what must you confirm?
questions.answer: The meats, with the kitchen
distractors: The rice variety, with the bar
questions.why: The menu prints no description, and recipes differ on which meats go in, so the kitchen answers before you describe it.

questions.q: What usually sets a Bavarian cream such as the one in The Snickers?
questions.answer: Gelatine in the custard
questions.why: A Bavarian cream is crème anglaise usually set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, so it holds its shape yet stays light; ask the kitchen for a guest who avoids gelatine.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature does a crème anglaise coat the spoon?
questions.why: The yolks thicken the custard at about 82°C (180°F); boiling sets them into curds and the anglaise turns grainy.

questions.q: Reading a plate by method, which question belongs on the list?
questions.answer: What is the cooking medium?
distractors: What does it cost to make?
Who on the line cooked it?
questions.why: Medium, heat and time, texture and the ticket are the four questions; the medium, steam, dry heat or fat, comes first.

questions.q: What makes the puff pastry of the Tarte Tatin rise?
questions.answer: Steam from its layered butter
questions.why: Puff pastry is laminated: the water in its butter turns to steam in the oven and pushes the layers apart, with no yeast at all.

steps.title: Build the Eggs Hussarde
steps.prompt: Put the stages of the Eggs Hussarde, poached ahead and stacked as the house guide gives it, in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Poach the eggs ahead in water just below a simmer, about 85°C (185°F), for about three minutes
Lift them into iced water and hold them until the order comes in
On the order, rewarm a held egg in hot water, well below a simmer, for 30 seconds to a minute, while the split English muffin toasts and the Canadian bacon warms
Lay the muffin on the plate and the Canadian bacon on the muffin
Spoon the hot marchand de vin over the bacon
Drain the warmed egg well and set it on the sauce
Spoon the warm hollandaise over the egg and send the plate at once
steps.distractor: Keep the poaching water at a rolling boil so the whites set faster
steps.why: Many kitchens poach ahead and hold the eggs cold, so the plate comes together in moments. The house guide stacks from the bottom: muffin, bacon, marchand de vin, egg, hollandaise, so the dark sauce sits under the egg and the pale one rests on it. A rolling boil tears the whites. Confirm the house stacking at the pass.

steps.title: Flame Bananas Foster at the table
steps.prompt: Put the stages of Bananas Foster at the guéridon, the tableside cart, in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Set the cart where nothing hangs overhead, the spirits measured into small vessels and a lid in reach
Melt the butter and brown sugar to a bubbling blond caramel and dust it with cinnamon
